user.label: Resource owner
user.summary: The human who owns the data and grants access
user.detail: The person clicking *Sign in with…*. OAuth's core promise to them: the client application never sees their password — only the authorization server does. Everything the user touches happens on the front channel, through the browser.

browser.label: Browser (user agent)
browser.summary: Carries the front channel: redirects anyone can observe
browser.detail: Every value that rides a redirect through the browser — URLs, query strings, history, extensions, shoulder-surfers — should be treated as visible and tamperable. The protocol is designed so nothing that passes through here is sufficient to obtain tokens by itself.

client_app.label: Client app (server)
client_app.summary: The application requesting access on the user's behalf
client_app.detail: A *confidential* client: it runs server-side and can keep a `client_secret`. It initiates the flow, receives the code on its registered redirect URI, and performs the back-channel exchange. Public clients (SPAs, mobile) run the same flow minus the secret — PKCE carries the proof instead.

auth_endpoint.label: Authorization endpoint
auth_endpoint.summary: Front-channel entry: authenticates the user, gathers consent
auth_endpoint.detail: Receives `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, and the PKCE `code_challenge`. It authenticates the **user** (not the client) and validates that `redirect_uri` exactly matches a registered value before anything else happens.

consent_page.label: Consent
consent_page.summary: The user approves the requested scopes
consent_page.detail: Where the resource owner sees *what* the client is asking for (`scope`) and says yes or no. Only after approval does the server mint an authorization code. Skipping meaningful consent is how confused-deputy problems start.

auth_code.label: Authorization code
auth_code.summary: Single-use, short-lived claim ticket — not a token
auth_code.detail: Worthless by itself: single-use, expires in minutes (the spec recommends ≤10), bound to the `client_id`, the exact `redirect_uri`, and the PKCE challenge. It exists so the *only* secret-bearing exchange can happen on the back channel.

token_endpoint.label: Token endpoint
token_endpoint.detail: Server-to-server only. Verifies the authorization code, the client's credentials (`client_secret` for confidential clients), and the PKCE `code_verifier` against the challenge sent earlier. Issues the access token and, optionally, a refresh token. Also serves `grant_type=refresh_token`.

pkce_verifier.label: PKCE verifier
pkce_verifier.summary: Per-request proof that the code redeemer started the flow
pkce_verifier.detail: The client generates a random `code_verifier`, sends its hash (`code_challenge`) on the front channel, and reveals the verifier only on the back channel. An attacker who intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier. Required for public clients; recommended for everyone.

redirect_uri.label: Registered redirect URI
redirect_uri.summary: Exact-match allowlist for where codes may be delivered
redirect_uri.detail: The authorization server delivers the code only to a pre-registered URI, compared **exactly** (no wildcards, no open redirects). This is the front channel's main defense: a stolen authorization request can't reroute the code to an attacker's server.

access_token.label: Access token
access_token.summary: Short-lived bearer credential shown to the API
access_token.detail: A *bearer* token: whoever holds it is authorized — the API validates the token, not the person. That is why it is deliberately short-lived (minutes to an hour): expiry is the blast-radius limit on leakage. Sent as `Authorization: Bearer …`.

refresh_token.label: Refresh token
refresh_token.summary: Long-lived secret shown ONLY to the token endpoint
refresh_token.detail: Lets the client mint new access tokens without re-involving the user. It is a long-lived, confidential credential: it never appears in an Authorization header, never goes to the resource server, and is often rotated on every use so a replay betrays the theft.

api.label: Resource server (API)
api.summary: Serves data to any bearer of a valid access token
api.detail: Validates the access token (signature/introspection, expiry, scope, audience) and serves the request. It never sees the user's password, the authorization code, or the refresh token. When the token expires it answers `401` — which is the design working, not failing.

scenes.title: Two channels, three credentials
scenes.claim: The whole design exists so the browser-visible channel never carries a real token.
scenes.annotation: Everything on the left rides redirects anyone can observe; everything that matters happens server-to-server on the right. Three credentials will appear — a code, an access token, a refresh token — each with a different lifetime and a different audience.
scenes.question: Before we zoom in: which of these boxes should never see an access token?

scenes.title: The front channel is hostile
scenes.claim: Everything passing through the browser is visible and tamperable — the exact-match redirect URI is the front channel's main defense.
scenes.annotation: The authorization request travels as a plain 302 with query parameters. The server will deliver the code only to a **pre-registered, exactly-matching** URI — so tampering with the request can't reroute the response to an attacker. `state` rides along to bind the response to the session that started it (CSRF).
scenes.misconception: The redirect is not a UX hop — it is the security boundary of the whole flow.

scenes.title: The code is a claim ticket
scenes.claim: The authorization code is deliberately worthless alone: single-use, minutes-long, and bound to client, redirect URI, and PKCE challenge.
scenes.annotation: Consent mints the code; the browser merely carries it home. Worked example: an attacker steals `?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA` from the URL. To redeem it they must present the client's secret AND the PKCE verifier that hashes to the challenge from step one — they have neither, and the code dies in minutes anyway.
scenes.question: Why is intercepting the code (mostly) useless to an attacker?

scenes.title: The back channel exchange
scenes.claim: The exchange happens server-to-server with three proofs at once: the code, the client secret, and the PKCE verifier.
scenes.annotation: One POST, three proofs: *the user approved this* (code), *I am the registered client* (secret), *I am the same party that started the flow* (verifier). Only after all three does the server issue tokens — and the browser never sees this request at all.
scenes.misconception: PKCE does not replace the client secret — it complements it, and stands in for it only on public clients that cannot keep one.

scenes.title: Tokens have different jobs
scenes.claim: The access token is a short-lived bearer pass shown to the API; the refresh token is a long-lived secret shown only to the token endpoint.
scenes.annotation: Bearer means bearer: the API authorizes whoever presents a valid token, no questions asked. That's tolerable because it expires quickly. The refresh token is the opposite trade — long-lived, so it must never travel to the API or appear in a header the resource server logs.
scenes.question: Why must the refresh token never appear in an Authorization header sent to the API?

scenes.title: Expiry is the design working
scenes.claim: The 401-then-refresh loop is intended behavior: short expiry bounds the blast radius of any leaked bearer token.
scenes.annotation: When the API answers `401`, the client silently exchanges the refresh token for a fresh access token and retries — no user interaction. Servers that rotate refresh tokens on every use get theft detection for free: a replayed old token proves someone else redeemed it.
scenes.transition: Now reassemble the whole flow with all three credentials in view.

scenes.title: What each channel carries
scenes.claim: Front channel: only the code. Back channel: the tokens. Expiry and rotation keep bearer risk bounded.
scenes.annotation: Judge any OAuth variant against this shape: does a real token ever touch the front channel? Does anything long-lived ever reach the resource server? The implicit flow died precisely because it answered *yes* to the first question.
scenes.question: A leaked access token vs a leaked refresh token: which hurts more, and which design choice limits each?

scenes.title: The nightclub with dissolving wristbands
scenes.claim: One story to keep: a hand stamp traded at the back office for a dissolving wristband, while the coat-check ticket stays in a locked drawer.
scenes.annotation: At the club door, the **doorman** checks your ID against the guest list and gives you a **hand stamp** — it smudges into nothing within minutes and only works once. You don't drink on a stamp: at the **back-office window** you trade it — while the manager checks the club's own ledger — for a **paper wristband that dissolves in an hour** and a **coat-check ticket they keep in a locked drawer**. Every **bartender** pours for anyone wearing a valid wristband; they never ask your name. When the wristband dissolves mid-night, you don't re-queue at the door — the coat-check ticket gets you a fresh one from the back office. Flash the ticket at a bartender, though, and security walks you out.

recallQuestions.prompt: Why does the bartender never learn your name?
recallQuestions.answer: Access tokens are bearer credentials — the API validates the token, not the person; possession is authorization, which is why expiry must be short.

recallQuestions.prompt: Your wristband just dissolved. Why don't you re-queue at the door?
recallQuestions.answer: The refresh grant: the client exchanges the long-lived refresh token at the token endpoint for a new access token — no user interaction, no re-consent.

relabel.access_token: Access token — minutes to 1 hour, bearer
relabel.refresh_token: Refresh token — days to months, confidential
